# Adjudication of the three reviewers' judgements: Hamido 2021

## D1: Randomization process
**Choice: C (Some concerns, same as B). Revised: Some concerns.**

- **Testing Reviewer A (High):** Figure 1 / Table 4 give High only if 1.2 is N/PN, or if 1.2 is NI and 1.3 is Y/PY.
  - Box 4, 1.2 allows "No" only "if there is reason to suspect that the enrolling investigator or the participant had knowledge of the forthcoming allocation."
  - A coin tossed "behind closed doors prior to the surgical appointments" (p.2) cannot be known before it is tossed. The real weakness is that the toss could have been repeated or overridden, and the article gives no information either way. That supports NI, not PN.
- **Testing a "Yes" on 1.2:** Box 4 accepts as "Yes" only a remote or central method, or envelopes used properly. Neither is described, so "Yes" also fails.
- **Baseline balance (1.3):** groups were 54 vs 53, and every baseline comparison was "n.s." (Tables 1–4).
  - The baseline tables cover only the 102 analysed patients, but that is 95% of those randomized.
  - The internal inconsistencies (a KT-1000 median outside its stated range) look like reporting errors, not imbalance.
  - Section 4.3.3.1 says chance imbalances "are not a source of systematic bias."
- **Route:** 1.2 NI → 1.3 PN → Some concerns (Table 4, row "Any response / NI / N/PN/NI").

## D2: Deviations from intended interventions (effect of assignment)
**Choice: B (Low, same as C). Revised: Low.**

- **Testing Reviewer A (Some concerns):** this needs 2.3 = NI, or a deviation answered PY at 2.3, or an inappropriate analysis.
- **Is NI right for 2.3?** Box 6 notes that "No information may be appropriate, because trialists do not always report whether deviations arose because of the trial context." Here, though:
  - The flow chart shows "Intervention (n = 107)", with no crossovers (Fig. 1).
  - The rehabilitation protocol was the same for both groups (p.3).
  - The only extra care reported (physiotherapy for arthrofibrosis, p.5) is protocol-consistent, because it treats a consequence of the intervention (Box 6, 2.3).
- **Unblinding alone is not enough:** section 5.1.2.1 says unblinding matters only when deviations "arose because of the trial context", and Box 6 requires "evidence, or strong reason to believe" before answering Yes.
- **I looked for other problems:**
  - Group A's gracilis was "set aside for possible augmentation if needed" (p.3). No use of it is reported, and it is a protocol option anyway.
  - Table 2 shows grade II preoperative pivot shifts, although inclusion required grade III. This is an eligibility inconsistency, not a deviation from the assigned intervention.
- **Analysis:** the 5 participants lost to follow-up were excluded and everyone else was analysed as randomized. That is an mITT analysis, which counts as appropriate ("mITT analyses excluding participants with missing outcome data should be considered appropriate", Box 6, 2.6). So 2.7 is NA.
- **Route:** Part 1 Low and Part 2 Low, so Low (Table 6).

## D4: Measurement of the outcome
**Choice: B (High). Revised: High.**

All three reviewers agree on the path up to 4.4 (assessors aware, assessment could have been influenced). The disagreement is only at 4.5. I tried to argue my way down to Some concerns using three points:

- **The examiner did not operate.** Section 7.3 says risk is "lower … if the outcome assessor is an independent researcher".
- **The comparator is an active intervention.** Section 7.3 says risk is "higher … if the comparator is no treatment."
- **KT-1000 is an instrumented test.**

None of these holds up well:

- **The examiner was not an independent researcher.** The contributions statement (p.7) says all authors but two participated in data collection. Most of those who did (YM, AS, WS, AN) also assisted in theatre. AAH collected data, co-designed the study and ran the statistics, but did not assist at surgery. So the surgeon who examined patients without having operated was most likely a study investigator, not an independent researcher.
- **The investigators' expectations are explicit.** They state a hypothesis favouring ALL reconstruction, write that its "importance … cannot be neglected" (p.6), and give the paper a title asserting benefit. Box 10, 4.5 says that when there are "strong levels of belief in … beneficial … effects … it is more likely that the outcome was influenced."
- **The active-comparator point does not apply.** Group B received ACL reconstruction plus an extra procedure, so the comparison is an add-on, not two competing active treatments. The examiner could also see that procedure's lateral incision (p.3).
- **The main component is subjective.** The authors themselves call the pivot shift "subjective and examiner dependent" (p.7), and the KT-1000 is also applied manually by an examiner.
- **Composite result:** section 7.1(5) says to weigh "the most influential components." Here the main subjective component is the pivot shift.

Reviewers A and C's Some concerns would mean there is "no reason to believe" assessment was influenced (Box 10, 4.5). These documents do give such reasons.

**Route:** Table 12, row N/PN, N/PN, Y/PY/NI, Y/PY/NI, Y/PY/NI → High.

## D5: Selection of the reported result
**Choice: C (Some concerns, same as B). Revised: Some concerns.**

- **Testing Reviewer A (Low):** Low requires 5.1 = Y/PY, and Table 13 requires "a pre-specified plan that was finalised before unblinded outcome data were available".
  - The documents contain no protocol, registry record or statistical analysis plan, only an IRB ID.
  - Section 8.3.1 asks for a "date-stamp" showing the plan came before unblinded data. With nothing available, 5.1 can only be NI, so Low cannot be supported.
- **Testing a High:** that needs 5.2 or 5.3 = Y/PY, which Box 11 ties to "clear evidence" of selection. There is none:
  - every measure listed in the Methods is reported, including null results (anterior drawer, Lachman, Lysholm, Tegner);
  - pivot shift is reported across all grades;
  - the tests used match those stated in the Methods (p.4).
- **5.2/5.3 may arguably be NI rather than PN,** because intentions are unavailable (Box 11 "No information" rule). Every combination of these answers without a Y/PY still leads to Some concerns (Table 14 / Figure 7).

CHOICE: D1=C; D2=B; D4=B; D5=C
REVISED: D1=Some concerns; D2=Low; D4=High; D5=Some concerns

# Adjudication of the three reviewers' judgements: Hamido 2021

## D1: Randomization process
**Choice: C (Some concerns, same as B). Revised: Some concerns.**

- **Testing Reviewer A (High):** Figure 1 / Table 4 give High only if 1.2 is N/PN, or if 1.2 is NI and 1.3 is Y/PY.
  - Box 4, 1.2 allows "No" only "if there is reason to suspect that the enrolling investigator or the participant had knowledge of the forthcoming allocation."
  - A coin tossed "behind closed doors prior to the surgical appointments" (p.2) cannot be known before it is tossed. The real weakness is that the toss could have been repeated or overridden, and the article gives no information either way. That supports NI, not PN.
- **Testing a "Yes" on 1.2:** Box 4 accepts as "Yes" only a remote or central method, or envelopes used properly. Neither is described, so "Yes" also fails.
- **Baseline balance (1.3):** groups were 54 vs 53, and every baseline comparison was "n.s." (Tables 1–4).
  - The baseline tables cover only the 102 analysed patients, but that is 95% of those randomized.
  - The internal inconsistencies (a KT-1000 median outside its stated range) look like reporting errors, not imbalance.
  - Section 4.3.3.1 says chance imbalances "are not a source of systematic bias."
- **Route:** 1.2 NI → 1.3 PN → Some concerns (Table 4, row "Any response / NI / N/PN/NI").

## D2: Deviations from intended interventions (effect of assignment)
**Choice: B (Low, same as C). Revised: Low.**

- **Testing Reviewer A (Some concerns):** this needs 2.3 = NI, or a deviation answered PY at 2.3, or an inappropriate analysis.
- **Is NI right for 2.3?** Box 6 notes that "No information may be appropriate, because trialists do not always report whether deviations arose because of the trial context." Here, though:
  - The flow chart shows "Intervention (n = 107)", with no crossovers (Fig. 1).
  - The rehabilitation protocol was the same for both groups (p.3).
  - The only extra care reported (physiotherapy for arthrofibrosis, p.5) is protocol-consistent, because it treats a consequence of the intervention (Box 6, 2.3).
- **Unblinding alone is not enough:** section 5.1.2.1 says unblinding matters only when deviations "arose because of the trial context", and Box 6 requires "evidence, or strong reason to believe" before answering Yes.
- **I looked for other problems:**
  - Group A's gracilis was "set aside for possible augmentation if needed" (p.3). No use of it is reported, and it is a protocol option anyway.
  - Table 2 shows grade II preoperative pivot shifts, although inclusion required grade III. This is an eligibility inconsistency, not a deviation from the assigned intervention.
- **Analysis:** the 5 participants lost to follow-up were excluded and everyone else was analysed as randomized. That is an mITT analysis, which counts as appropriate ("mITT analyses excluding participants with missing outcome data should be considered appropriate", Box 6, 2.6). So 2.7 is NA.
- **Route:** Part 1 Low and Part 2 Low, so Low (Table 6).

## D4: Measurement of the outcome
**Choice: B (High). Revised: High.**

All three reviewers agree on the path up to 4.4 (assessors aware, assessment could have been influenced). The disagreement is only at 4.5. I tried to argue my way down to Some concerns using three points:

- **The examiner did not operate.** Section 7.3 says risk is "lower … if the outcome assessor is an independent researcher".
- **The comparator is an active intervention.** Section 7.3 says risk is "higher … if the comparator is no treatment."
- **KT-1000 is an instrumented test.**

None of these holds up well:

- **The examiner was not an independent researcher.** The contributions statement (p.7) says all authors but two participated in data collection. Most of those who did (YM, AS, WS, AN) also assisted in theatre. AAH collected data, co-designed the study and ran the statistics, but did not assist at surgery. So the surgeon who examined patients without having operated was most likely a study investigator, not an independent researcher.
- **The investigators' expectations are explicit.** They state a hypothesis favouring ALL reconstruction, write that its "importance … cannot be neglected" (p.6), and give the paper a title asserting benefit. Box 10, 4.5 says that when there are "strong levels of belief in … beneficial … effects … it is more likely that the outcome was influenced."
- **The active-comparator point does not apply.** Group B received ACL reconstruction plus an extra procedure, so the comparison is an add-on, not two competing active treatments. The examiner could also see that procedure's lateral incision (p.3).
- **The main component is subjective.** The authors themselves call the pivot shift "subjective and examiner dependent" (p.7), and the KT-1000 is also applied manually by an examiner.
- **Composite result:** section 7.1(5) says to weigh "the most influential components." Here the main subjective component is the pivot shift.

Reviewers A and C's Some concerns would mean there is "no reason to believe" assessment was influenced (Box 10, 4.5). These documents do give such reasons.

**Route:** Table 12, row N/PN, N/PN, Y/PY/NI, Y/PY/NI, Y/PY/NI → High.

## D5: Selection of the reported result
**Choice: C (Some concerns, same as B). Revised: Some concerns.**

- **Testing Reviewer A (Low):** Low requires 5.1 = Y/PY, and Table 13 requires "a pre-specified plan that was finalised before unblinded outcome data were available".
  - The documents contain no protocol, registry record or statistical analysis plan, only an IRB ID.
  - Section 8.3.1 asks for a "date-stamp" showing the plan came before unblinded data. With nothing available, 5.1 can only be NI, so Low cannot be supported.
- **Testing a High:** that needs 5.2 or 5.3 = Y/PY, which Box 11 ties to "clear evidence" of selection. There is none:
  - every measure listed in the Methods is reported, including null results (anterior drawer, Lachman, Lysholm, Tegner);
  - pivot shift is reported across all grades;
  - the tests used match those stated in the Methods (p.4).
- **5.2/5.3 may arguably be NI rather than PN,** because intentions are unavailable (Box 11 "No information" rule). Every combination of these answers without a Y/PY still leads to Some concerns (Table 14 / Figure 7).

CHOICE: D1=C; D2=B; D4=B; D5=C
REVISED: D1=Some concerns; D2=Low; D4=High; D5=Some concerns

**D1 — High (Reviewer A; C is equally defensible).** The strongest argument against High is that distributing coded lists does not prove recruiters could interpret forthcoming assignments. **D2 — Low (Reviewer C).** B’s High could follow from interpreting the completer analysis as an inappropriate per-protocol analysis, but the reported exclusions correspond to attrition, with no evidence that available outcomes were discarded for non-adherence or reassigned between groups (Figure 1; Table 2). Section 5.3.1 explicitly treats analyses excluding missing outcomes as appropriate for D2. A’s Some concerns is plausible if trial-context deviations are genuinely unknown. However, the article supplies explanatory evidence: limited app use, participants’ low perceived need for care, and promoters’ difficulties adapting their communication style (p.8). These support ordinary engagement and implementation difficulties rather than trial-induced departures. Challenging my earlier assessment, absence of reported contamination alone would not justify Low; here, the reported circumstances support PN. Box 6, 2.3 requires evidence or strong reason linking departures to the trial context and allows PN for difficulties consistent with practice outside trials. With 2.6=PY, Table 6 proposes Low.

**D3 — High (Reviewer A; B is equally defensible).** C’s Some concerns correctly challenges any inference based solely on the large attrition percentage: magnitude alone does not establish outcome-dependent missingness (§6.1.3.2). Pregnancy losses were also similar between groups—77 versus 84—and some other losses were logistical (Figure 1). However, pregnancy accounts for 161 of 243 missing endpoints and directly affects the waist circumference that would have been measured. That supports **likely**, rather than merely possible, dependence on the true outcome under Box 8, 3.4, reason 2. Neither planned pregnancy exclusions nor broadly balanced losses establish absence of bias; §6.1.3 explains that outcome-dependent missingness can bias continuous-outcome comparisons even without differential missingness between arms. No suitable sensitivity analysis is reported. Figure 4 therefore supports High through N/N/Y/PY, independently of concerns about the analysis in D2.

However, manually locating and measuring waist circumference involves some judgement, unlike an automated measurement; standardization reduces that discretion without eliminating it. Assessor blinding is not reported, and the registry specifies no masking, supporting probable awareness. Section 7.1’s observer-outcome category involving some judgement and Box 10, 4.4 therefore support possible influence. Conversely, separate assessors, training and standardized procedures argue against **likely** material influence under §7.3 and Box 10, 4.5. **D1 — High (Reviewer A; C is equally defensible).** The strongest argument against High is that distributing coded lists does not prove recruiters could interpret forthcoming assignments. Nevertheless, the enrolling nurse selected the lowest available ID from locally supplied lists containing randomisation codes, with fixed blocks of six and no described access safeguards (article p.3). Blinding the authors does not establish concealment from recruiters. Box 4, question 1.2, requires “reason to suspect” foreknowledge, rather than proof of manipulation; §4.3.2 also identifies predictable fixed-block allocation as problematic. Thus PN for concealment is more defensible than NI, rejecting B’s Some concerns under Figure 1. Conversely, the baseline age difference does **not** independently justify High: Table 1 covers completers only, warranting NI for 1.3 under Box 4.

**D2 — Low (Reviewer C).** B’s High could follow from interpreting the completer analysis as an inappropriate per-protocol analysis, but the reported exclusions correspond to attrition, with no evidence that available outcomes were discarded for non-adherence or reassigned between groups (Figure 1; Table 2). Section 5.3.1 explicitly treats analyses excluding missing outcomes as appropriate for D2. A’s Some concerns is plausible if trial-context deviations are genuinely unknown. However, the article supplies explanatory evidence: limited app use, participants’ low perceived need for care, and promoters’ difficulties adapting their communication style (p.8). These support ordinary engagement and implementation difficulties rather than trial-induced departures. Challenging my earlier assessment, absence of reported contamination alone would not justify Low; here, the reported circumstances support PN. Box 6, 2.3 requires evidence or strong reason linking departures to the trial context and allows PN for difficulties consistent with practice outside trials. With 2.6=PY, Table 6 proposes Low.

**D3 — High (Reviewer A; B is equally defensible).** C’s Some concerns correctly challenges any inference based solely on the large attrition percentage: magnitude alone does not establish outcome-dependent missingness (§6.1.3.2). Pregnancy losses were also similar between groups—77 versus 84—and some other losses were logistical (Figure 1). However, pregnancy accounts for 161 of 243 missing endpoints and directly affects the waist circumference that would have been measured. That supports **likely**, rather than merely possible, dependence on the true outcome under Box 8, 3.4, reason 2. Neither planned pregnancy exclusions nor broadly balanced losses establish absence of bias; §6.1.3 explains that outcome-dependent missingness can bias continuous-outcome comparisons even without differential missingness between arms. No suitable sensitivity analysis is reported. Figure 4 therefore supports High through N/N/Y/PY, independently of concerns about the analysis in D2.

**D4 — Some concerns (Reviewer A; C is equally defensible).** B’s Low has substantial support: trained nurses used standardized WHO STEPS procedures and were separate from intervention providers (article p.3). My earlier judgement would be too severe if waist measurement involved effectively no assessor discretion. However, manually locating and measuring waist circumference involves some judgement, unlike an automated measurement; standardization reduces that discretion without eliminating it. Assessor blinding is not reported, and the registry specifies no masking, supporting probable awareness. Section 7.1’s observer-outcome category involving some judgement and Box 10, 4.4 therefore support possible influence. Conversely, separate assessors, training and standardized procedures argue against **likely** material influence under §7.3 and Box 10, 4.5. Figure 5 consequently supports Some concerns through N/PN/PY/PY/PN.

**D1 — High (Reviewer A; C is equally defensible).** The strongest argument against High is that distributing coded lists does not prove recruiters could interpret forthcoming assignments. Nevertheless, the enrolling nurse selected the lowest available ID from locally supplied lists containing randomisation codes, with fixed blocks of six and no described access safeguards (article p.3). Blinding the authors does not establish concealment from recruiters. Box 4, question 1.2, requires “reason to suspect” foreknowledge, rather than proof of manipulation; §4.3.2 also identifies predictable fixed-block allocation as problematic. Thus PN for concealment is more defensible than NI, rejecting B’s Some concerns under Figure 1. Conversely, the baseline age difference does **not** independently justify High: Table 1 covers completers only, warranting NI for 1.3 under Box 4.

**D2 — Low (Reviewer C).** B’s High could follow from interpreting the completer analysis as an inappropriate per-protocol analysis, but the reported exclusions correspond to attrition, with no evidence that available outcomes were discarded for non-adherence or reassigned between groups (Figure 1; Table 2). Section 5.3.1 explicitly treats analyses excluding missing outcomes as appropriate for D2. A’s Some concerns is plausible if trial-context deviations are genuinely unknown. However, the article supplies explanatory evidence: limited app use, participants’ low perceived need for care, and promoters’ difficulties adapting their communication style (p.8). These support ordinary engagement and implementation difficulties rather than trial-induced departures. Challenging my earlier assessment, absence of reported contamination alone would not justify Low; here, the reported circumstances support PN. Box 6, 2.3 requires evidence or strong reason linking departures to the trial context and allows PN for difficulties consistent with practice outside trials. With 2.6=PY, Table 6 proposes Low.

**D3 — High (Reviewer A; B is equally defensible).** C’s Some concerns correctly challenges any inference based solely on the large attrition percentage: magnitude alone does not establish outcome-dependent missingness (§6.1.3.2). Pregnancy losses were also similar between groups—77 versus 84—and some other losses were logistical (Figure 1). However, pregnancy accounts for 161 of 243 missing endpoints and directly affects the waist circumference that would have been measured. That supports **likely**, rather than merely possible, dependence on the true outcome under Box 8, 3.4, reason 2. Neither planned pregnancy exclusions nor broadly balanced losses establish absence of bias; §6.1.3 explains that outcome-dependent missingness can bias continuous-outcome comparisons even without differential missingness between arms. No suitable sensitivity analysis is reported. Figure 4 therefore supports High through N/N/Y/PY, independently of concerns about the analysis in D2.

**D4 — Some concerns (Reviewer A; C is equally defensible).** B’s Low has substantial support: trained nurses used standardized WHO STEPS procedures and were separate from intervention providers (article p.3). My earlier judgement would be too severe if waist measurement involved effectively no assessor discretion. However, manually locating and measuring waist circumference involves some judgement, unlike an automated measurement; standardization reduces that discretion without eliminating it. Assessor blinding is not reported, and the registry specifies no masking, supporting probable awareness. Section 7.1’s observer-outcome category involving some judgement and Box 10, 4.4 therefore support possible influence. Conversely, separate assessors, training and standardized procedures argue against **likely** material influence under §7.3 and Box 10, 4.5. Figure 5 consequently supports Some concerns through N/PN/PY/PY/PN.

A Probably no on 1.2 leads straight to High (Table 4, row "Any response / N/PN / Any response → High"). I also looked for a reason to override, under §4.4's allowance for overrides. None is listed as excluded for non-adherence while still measured. Box 6, 2.6 says "mITT analyses excluding participants with missing outcome data should be considered appropriate". §6.1 counts women who "can no longer experience the outcome" (here, pregnant women) as missing outcome data, which belongs in D3. The only clear non-adherence-type exclusion is 3 phone-incompatible women, about 1%. Even if that made 2.6 Probably no, 2.7 would be Probably no, giving Some concerns, not High. So B fails.

A's Some concerns could also come from Part 1, with 2.3 = NI ("may be appropriate, because trialists do not always report…"). Against that, Box 6 says to answer Yes "only if there is evidence, or strong reason to believe, that the trial context led to failure to implement". The reported fidelity problems are that CHPs were uncomfortable and the app was little used (p.8). Those would happen outside a trial too, so they get No/Probably no. I accept that A's reading is a reasonable alternative. Still, the rubric's default for an unreported problem the question looks for is "no evidence of that problem" (§1.1), which supports **Low**.

**D3 (A/B High vs C Some concerns).** C's Some concerns needs 3.4 to be No/Probably no. The best case for C: pregnancy, the main reason for missing data, was balanced (77 vs 84), and the proportions missing differ only modestly (53% vs 58% analysed). But Box 8, 3.4 lists "Reported reasons for missing outcome data differ between the intervention groups" as a reason for Yes. Figure 1 shows withdrawal 23 vs 14, lost to follow-up 12 vs 5, and phone incompatibility 3 vs 0 (only possible in the intervention arm). However, pregnancy accounts for 161 of 243 missing endpoints and directly affects the waist circumference that would have been measured. **D1 — High (Reviewer A; C is equally defensible).** The strongest argument against High is that distributing coded lists does not prove recruiters could interpret forthcoming assignments. Nevertheless, the enrolling nurse selected the lowest available ID from locally supplied lists containing randomisation codes, with fixed blocks of six and no described access safeguards (article p.3). Blinding the authors does not establish concealment from recruiters. Box 4, question 1.2, requires “reason to suspect” foreknowledge, rather than proof of manipulation; §4.3.2 also identifies predictable fixed-block allocation as problematic. Thus PN for concealment is more defensible than NI, rejecting B’s Some concerns under Figure 1. Conversely, the baseline age difference does **not** independently justify High: Table 1 covers completers only, warranting NI for 1.3 under Box 4.

**D2 — Low (Reviewer C).** B’s High could follow from interpreting the completer analysis as an inappropriate per-protocol analysis, but the reported exclusions correspond to attrition, with no evidence that available outcomes were discarded for non-adherence or reassigned between groups (Figure 1; Table 2). Section 5.3.1 explicitly treats analyses excluding missing outcomes as appropriate for D2. A’s Some concerns is plausible if trial-context deviations are genuinely unknown. However, the article supplies explanatory evidence: limited app use, participants’ low perceived need for care, and promoters’ difficulties adapting their communication style (p.8). These support ordinary engagement and implementation difficulties rather than trial-induced departures. Challenging my earlier assessment, absence of reported contamination alone would not justify Low; here, the reported circumstances support PN. Box 6, 2.3 requires evidence or strong reason linking departures to the trial context and allows PN for difficulties consistent with practice outside trials. With 2.6=PY, Table 6 proposes Low.

**D3 — High (Reviewer A; B is equally defensible).** C’s Some concerns correctly challenges any inference based solely on the large attrition percentage: magnitude alone does not establish outcome-dependent missingness (§6.1.3.2). Pregnancy losses were also similar between groups—77 versus 84—and some other losses were logistical (Figure 1). However, pregnancy accounts for 161 of 243 missing endpoints and directly affects the waist circumference that would have been measured. That supports **likely**, rather than merely possible, dependence on the true outcome under Box 8, 3.4, reason 2. Neither planned pregnancy exclusions nor broadly balanced losses establish absence of bias; §6.1.3 explains that outcome-dependent missingness can bias continuous-outcome comparisons even without differential missingness between arms. No suitable sensitivity analysis is reported. Figure 4 therefore supports High through N/N/Y/PY, independently of concerns about the analysis in D2.

**D4 — Some concerns (Reviewer A; C is equally defensible).** B’s Low has substantial support: trained nurses used standardized WHO STEPS procedures and were separate from intervention providers (article p.3). My earlier judgement would be too severe if waist measurement involved effectively no assessor discretion. However, manually locating and measuring waist circumference involves some judgement, unlike an automated measurement; standardization reduces that discretion without eliminating it. Assessor blinding is not reported, and the registry specifies no masking, supporting probable awareness. Section 7.1’s observer-outcome category involving some judgement and Box 10, 4.4 therefore support possible influence. Conversely, separate assessors, training and standardized procedures argue against **likely** material influence under §7.3 and Box 10, 4.5. Figure 5 consequently supports Some concerns through N/PN/PY/PY/PN.

CHOICE: D1=A; D2=C; D3=A; D4=A
REVISED: D1=High; D2=Low; D3=High; D4=Some concerns
adjudication_explanation_Z:
# Adjudication of the three reviewers' RoB 2 judgements for Hanafiah 2022, change in waist circumference

My revised judgements are the same as my first assessment: **D1 High, D2 Low, D3 High, D4 Some concerns**. After trying to break each reviewer's judgement, and my own, A's D1/D3/D4 and C's D2 held up best. Where two reviewers agree, I picked one letter; the agreement itself didn't count as evidence.

**D1 (A/C High vs B Some concerns).** B's Some concerns only works if 1.2 is "No information" and 1.3 is No/Probably no/NI (Table 4, row "Any response / NI / N/PN/NI"). The strongest case for B is that "randomisation codes" might have been neutral labels such as A/B rather than arm names, so the enrolling nurse might not have seen the next arm. I tested that. Even with neutral codes, this was an open trial ("non-blinded", p.2; registry "Masking: NONE"), so each assignment became known as soon as the participant started her arm. Blocks were a fixed six per clinic, and the nurse working through the list assigned "the lowest available ID number" (p.3). §4.3.2 covers exactly this: "When blocking is used… This will be a problem when the person recruiting participants knows the start and end of each block and the allocations are revealed after assignment… more serious if block sizes are small and of equal sizes. In such situations, an answer of 'No' or 'Probably no' should be provided." So the guidance itself calls for Probably no, not "No information". A Probably no on 1.2 leads straight to High (Table 4, row "Any response / N/PN / Any response → High"). I also looked for a reason to override, under §4.4's allowance for overrides. I found none: baseline data exist only for completers (1.3 = NI), so they can't reassure. **High stands.**

**D2 (C Low vs A Some concerns vs B High).** B's High needs 2.6 to be No/Probably no/NI and 2.7 to be Yes/Probably yes/NI (Table 6, Part 2). That would mean the analysis was effectively per-protocol with a substantial impact. The strongest hint is Figure 1's label "6 contact points and endpoint visit (n=145)". But the attrition boxes account for all 127 + 116 excluded women by reason: pregnancy, lost to follow-up, withdrawal, health, moved, phone incompatibility. None is listed as excluded for non-adherence while still measured. Box 6, 2.6 says "mITT analyses excluding participants with missing outcome data should be considered appropriate". §6.1 counts women who "can no longer experience the outcome" (here, pregnant women) as missing outcome data, which belongs in D3. The only clear non-adherence-type exclusion is 3 phone-incompatible women, about 1%. Even if that made 2.6 Probably no, 2.7 would be Probably no, giving Some concerns, not High. So B fails.

A's Some concerns could also come from Part 1, with 2.3 = NI ("may be appropriate, because trialists do not always report…"). Against that, Box 6 says to answer Yes "only if there is evidence, or strong reason to believe, that the trial context led to failure to implement". The reported fidelity problems are that CHPs were uncomfortable and the app was little used (p.8). Those would happen outside a trial too, so they get No/Probably no. I accept that A's reading is a reasonable alternative. Still, the rubric's default for an unreported problem the question looks for is "no evidence of that problem" (§1.1), which supports **Low**.

**D3 (A/B High vs C Some concerns).** C's Some concerns needs 3.4 to be No/Probably no. The best case for C: pregnancy, the main reason for missing data, was balanced (77 vs 84), and the proportions missing differ only modestly (53% vs 58% analysed). But Box 8, 3.4 lists "Reported reasons for missing outcome data differ between the intervention groups" as a reason for Yes. Figure 1 shows withdrawal 23 vs 14, lost to follow-up 12 vs 5, and phone incompatibility 3 vs 0 (only possible in the intervention arm). Reason 4 (trial circumstances) also applies: in adiposity trials, dropout plausibly tracks weight trajectory, and 44% of outcomes are missing with no sensitivity analysis (so 3.2 = N). Table 10, row "N/PN/NI; N/PN; Y/PY/NI; Y/PY/NI → High". **High stands.**

**D4 (A/C Some concerns vs B Low).** For Low, B needs either 4.3 = No (blinded assessors) or 4.4 = No (assessment couldn't be influenced). Nothing reports blinding of the study nurses, and the registry says "Masking: NONE". Box 10, 4.3 says answer No only "if outcome assessors were blinded". For 4.4, B could argue that waist circumference is objective. But it is a manual tape measurement, which involves placement, tension and reading. That fits §7.1(5) category 3, "observer-reported outcomes involving some judgement", not category 2 (e.g. "the result of an automated test"). Concluding influence was likely (4.5 = Yes) would be too strong given the WHO STEPS protocol and data collectors separate from the intervention team, so 4.5 = Probably no. Table 12 → **Some concerns**.

CHOICE: D1=A; D2=C; D3=A; D4=A
REVISED: D1=High; D2=Low; D3=High; D4=Some concerns

## D1: randomization process (A = Some concerns; B, C = Low)

To make A's case, I tested my own "Probably yes" on 1.2. Allocation concealment is not the same as blinding. The guidance warns that concealment "should not be confused with blinding of assigned interventions during the trial" (§4.1). Identical pharmacy-made capsules prove blinding after assignment, not concealment before it. No document says who generated or held the list. If the PI generated it and passed it to the pharmacy, the PI could have known the sequence, and the stratification by daily vs non-daily use could have used small predictable blocks. That supports "No information", which leads to Some concerns (Table 4 row "Any / NI / N/PN/NI").

Against A, the evidence goes beyond "a placebo was used":
- The article says the "McLean Research Pharmacy prepared capsules that contained either nabilone or placebo" (p.2).
- The protocol (§8.3.1.b) says staff "present 7 day prescriptions to the McLean pharmacy". In other words, staff order the trial drug and the pharmacy fills it with active drug or placebo, so the allocation sits with the pharmacy.
- The registry lists the investigator as masked.

Box 4 (1.2) says to answer Yes where "the process of allocation is controlled by an external unit … (e.g. independent central pharmacy)". It also says "a judgement may be required to justify an answer of 'Probably yes'". §1.1 limits "No information" to cases where it "would be unreasonable to respond 'Probably yes'". A pharmacy-held code combined with a masked investigator makes "Probably yes" reasonable, though not certain. Baseline groups (10 vs 8; all Table 1 p ≥ 0.15) are compatible with chance. Low is the more defensible judgement, but A's position is close behind.

## D3: missing outcome data (A = Low; B, C = Some concerns)

The best case for A runs like this:
- Adverse events were collected at every visit "from the time the subject was randomized up until the subject's last visit" (registry).
- All randomized participants are counted as at risk.
- The pregnant participant was followed to the end.
- No one stopped medication because of adverse events (p.4).

On that basis 3.3 could be "Probably no" under Box 8: "if all missing outcome data occurred for documented reasons that are unrelated to the outcome then the risk of bias … will be low".

That rule needs all reasons to be documented and unrelated, and here they are not:
- "No longer interested" (2, nabilone) and "Lost to follow-up" (1, placebo) could reflect tolerability.
- The article text contradicts Fig. 1 ("withdrawn by study staff due to repeated missed visits").
- When dropouts left is not reported.

§6.1.5 says withdrawn participants "should be regarded as having missing outcome data, even though some of their follow up is included". Box 8 (3.1) says missing data are only negligible when "the observed number of events is much greater than the number of participants with missing outcome data". Here 5 participants had incomplete follow-up and only 6 had any event, so 3.1 cannot be Yes. The missing proportions are similar between arms and most reasons are not health-related, so 3.4 is "Probably no", not Yes. That leaves Some concerns (Table 10, row 4). A's Low depends on an unsupported 3.3 answer.

## D5: selection of the reported result (A, C = Some concerns; B = Low)

Low requires 5.1 to be Yes or "Probably yes" (Table 14, row 1; Table 13 "Low": "analysed in accordance with a pre-specified plan that was finalised before unblinded outcome data were available"). No document meets that standard:
- The 2011 registry primary outcomes are cannabis-use measures, with no adverse-event outcome.
- The only protocol/SAP is dated 4/14/17, after the data existed, and has no adverse-event analysis.
- The article then calls adverse events the "primary hypothesis".

§8.3.1 requires a "'date-stamp' confirming that the analysis intentions were finalized before unblinded outcome data were available". B's Low is therefore against the rubric.

- The protocol collected an Adverse Events Checklist and the FISER/GRSEB rating (§8.3.2.a), but neither is reported.

Box 11 asks for "clear evidence … and the fully reported result is likely to have been selected on the basis of the results". ## D1: randomization process (A = Some concerns; B, C = Low)

To make A's case, I tested my own "Probably yes" on 1.2. Allocation concealment is not the same as blinding. The guidance warns that concealment "should not be confused with blinding of assigned interventions during the trial" (§4.1). Identical pharmacy-made capsules prove blinding after assignment, not concealment before it. No document says who generated or held the list. If the PI generated it and passed it to the pharmacy, the PI could have known the sequence, and the stratification by daily vs non-daily use could have used small predictable blocks. That supports "No information", which leads to Some concerns (Table 4 row "Any / NI / N/PN/NI").

Against A, the evidence goes beyond "a placebo was used":
- The article says the "McLean Research Pharmacy prepared capsules that contained either nabilone or placebo" (p.2).
- The protocol (§8.3.1.b) says staff "present 7 day prescriptions to the McLean pharmacy". In other words, staff order the trial drug and the pharmacy fills it with active drug or placebo, so the allocation sits with the pharmacy.
- The registry lists the investigator as masked.

Box 4 (1.2) says to answer Yes where "the process of allocation is controlled by an external unit … (e.g. independent central pharmacy)". It also says "a judgement may be required to justify an answer of 'Probably yes'". §1.1 limits "No information" to cases where it "would be unreasonable to respond 'Probably yes'". A pharmacy-held code combined with a masked investigator makes "Probably yes" reasonable, though not certain. Baseline groups (10 vs 8; all Table 1 p ≥ 0.15) are compatible with chance. Low is the more defensible judgement, but A's position is close behind.

## D3: missing outcome data (A = Low; B, C = Some concerns)

The best case for A runs like this:
- Adverse events were collected at every visit "from the time the subject was randomized up until the subject's last visit" (registry).
- All randomized participants are counted as at risk.
- The pregnant participant was followed to the end.
- No one stopped medication because of adverse events (p.4).

On that basis 3.3 could be "Probably no" under Box 8: "if all missing outcome data occurred for documented reasons that are unrelated to the outcome then the risk of bias … will be low".

That rule needs all reasons to be documented and unrelated, and here they are not:
- "No longer interested" (2, nabilone) and "Lost to follow-up" (1, placebo) could reflect tolerability.
- The article text contradicts Fig. 1 ("withdrawn by study staff due to repeated missed visits").
- When dropouts left is not reported.

§6.1.5 says withdrawn participants "should be regarded as having missing outcome data, even though some of their follow up is included". Box 8 (3.1) says missing data are only negligible when "the observed number of events is much greater than the number of participants with missing outcome data". Here 5 participants had incomplete follow-up and only 6 had any event, so 3.1 cannot be Yes. - The 2011 registry primary outcomes are cannabis-use measures, with no adverse-event outcome.
- The only protocol/SAP is dated 4/14/17, after the data existed, and has no adverse-event analysis.
- The article then calls adverse events the "primary hypothesis".

- **Experimental intervention:** clopidogrel 75 mg once daily.
- **Comparator:** aspirin 100 mg once daily.
- **Result assessed:** the 24-month primary composite. Events were 152 (5.7%) with clopidogrel and 207 (7.7%) with aspirin; HR 0.73 (95% CI 0.59–0.90) in the ITT population (Table 2, p 2491; Figure 2A).
- **Effect of interest:** effect of assignment to intervention (ITT).
- **Sources used:** journal article, supplementary appendix (which contains the protocol and statistical analysis plan) and the ClinicalTrials.gov record NCT02044250.

**Which components drive the composite** (Table 2), clopidogrel vs aspirin:

| Component | Clopidogrel | Aspirin |
|---|---|---|
| Readmission for acute coronary syndrome (ACS) | 66 | 109 |
| Major bleeding (BARC ≥3) | 33 | 53 |
| All-cause death | 51 | 36 |
| Stroke | 18 | 43 |
| Non-fatal MI | 18 | 28 |

- Every component uses a standard, prespecified definition: the third universal definition of MI, BARC bleeding classes, and explicit criteria for stroke and for readmission due to ACS (appendix pp 13–16).
- "On each visit, active surveillance was done for any adverse clinical events" (p 2489, Procedures).
- "The vital status of all patients was cross-checked through the National Health Insurance Service system … and the South Korea National Statistics System" (p 2489).

**4.2 Could measurement or ascertainment of the outcome have differed between groups? — PN**
- Evidence against a difference: both arms had the same follow-up schedule, "scheduled at 12 months and 24 months" (p 2489). The protocol adds that "when a patient does not appear … an investigator or research coordinator checks his/her status via telephone visits to minimize the risk of underreporting" (appendix p 53). Both arms had the same visit content (appendix pp 54–56) and the same national-database check of deaths.
- Evidence for a concern: aspirin causes more minor GI symptoms (272 vs 320, Table 2), which could lead to more investigations in the aspirin group. However, BARC ≥3 requires overt bleeding with a haemoglobin drop of at least 3 g/dL, a transfusion, surgery, or intracranial bleeding (appendix pp 15–16). This makes detection of symptomless events unlikely.

**4.3 Were outcome assessors aware of the intervention received? — PY**
- Evidence against awareness: final classification was by an "independent clinical-event committee whose members were unaware of the trial group assignments… received medical records… after removal of any reference to the treatment groups" (p 2488). The protocol says the same (appendix p 59).

- Most of the composite's events are not "observer-reported outcomes not involving judgement." Readmission for ACS is a provider decision (hospitalisation), and MI and stroke "require judgements based on medical records."

**D4 – Bias in measurement of the outcome.** I tried to knock down each judgement.

**The case for Low (Reviewers B and C).** It is not weak. §7.1(3) names "an adjudication committee" as a kind of outcome assessor. The Box 10 elaboration for 4.3 says "Answer 'No' if outcome assessors were blinded to intervention status." Here, every event was adjudicated by a committee "unaware of the trial group assignments" that worked from records "after removal of any reference to the treatment groups" (p 2488; appendix p 59). Under Table 12, 4.3 = N/PN leads straight to Low.

**Where that reasoning fails.** It treats the committee as the only assessor. That is not true for the component that drives this result.
- Readmission for ACS accounts for 66 vs 109 of the 152 vs 207 events (Table 2), with HR 0.61.
- §7.1 item 4 lists "hospitalization" as an outcome reflecting "decisions made by the intervention provider." It states that "the outcome assessor here is the care provider making the decision," and that such outcomes are "usually likely to be influenced by knowledge of intervention received, if the care provider is aware of this."
- §7.1 item 5 says assessment of a composite should "take into account the risk of bias due to the most influential components."
- A blinded committee can only judge events that reach it. The registry says "All endpoints will be assessed primarily by the investigator and adjudicated secondarily," and both participants and investigators were unmasked (p 2489; registry "Masking: NONE").
- The authors themselves concede "potential for bias in outcome reporting and ascertainment" and a "possibility of … under-reporting of events" (p 2495).
- National-registry verification covers only death, the one component that cannot be influenced.

So 4.3 and 4.4 are reasonably Y/PY for the most important component, and Low overstates what blinded adjudication protects.

**Could it be High (testing my own view)?** For 4.5 = Y, the Box 10 elaboration asks for "strong levels of belief in either beneficial or harmful effects." There is little sign of that:
- Both arms received an active standard drug, which §7.3 says carries lower risk than a usual-care comparator.
- Readmission required objective ACS criteria checked by the blinded committee.
- Follow-up and surveillance were the same in both arms.
- No differential reporting was documented.

So influence is possible but not likely: 4.5 = PN. That is the Table 12 row "N/PN, N/PN, Y/PY/NI, Y/PY/NI, N/PN → Some concerns." Table 11 describes exactly this case for Some concerns: assessment "could have been influenced" but "it is unlikely that" it was.

**Conclusion.** Blinded adjudication is real protection, which is why the result isn't High. It doesn't remove the influence of unblinded staff on the readmission decisions and event reports that make up most of the composite. I keep my judgement and choose Reviewer A.

CHOICE: D4=A
REVISED: D4=Some concerns

Section 4.1.2 identifies a known deterministic rule as a concealment failure, and Box 4, 1.1 explicitly rejects allocation by birth date. Figure 1 routes 1.2=N directly to High. **D2 — C, Low.** A/B’s Some concerns could follow from answering 2.3=NI: participants and surgeons knew treatment, and detailed monitoring of deviations is absent. I reconsidered whether my earlier PN inferred too much from silence. Nevertheless, the article provides affirmative evidence of assigned surgery delivery for all 110 participants and describes a common rehabilitation regimen, including clinically indicated modifications for meniscal repair (pp. 2–4). Together these support PN, although not definitive N, for trial-context deviations. Box 6, 2.3 requires evidence or strong reason to attribute deviations to trial context; awareness alone is insufficient. Figure 1 and the outcome tables also support analysis by assignment, excluding only missing follow-up. Section 5.3.1 explicitly accepts such exclusions within D2. Figure 2 therefore gives Low through 2.3=PN and 2.6=PY.

**D4 — A, Some concerns.** B/C’s Low is persuasive for KT-1000 and pivot shift: a separate surgeon assessed patients with stockings concealing the operated knees (p. 2). However, the requested result also includes subjective function, including Lysholm, and participants explicitly knew their treatment (p. 8). Box 10, 4.3 and §7.1 make the participant the assessor for participant-reported outcomes; a blinded examiner cannot remove that concern. Conversely, High would require likely influence, not merely possible influence. The active surgical comparator, separate examiner and approximately 27-month assessment support 4.5=PN under §7.3. No supplied protocol or dated analysis plan verifies decisions before unblinded data became available. Section 8.3.1 requires that timing, while Box 11, 5.2–5.3 specifies NI when intentions are insufficient and multiple measurements or analyses are possible. Figure 7 routes those NI answers to Some concerns. Neither multiple outcomes nor the significant KT-1000 result alone establishes High; A and B are equally defensible.

# Adjudication of three reviewers' RoB 2 judgements: Ibrahim et al. 2017

My judgements are unchanged after trying to overturn each one: D1 High, D2 Low, D4 Some concerns, D5 Some concerns. Reviewer A is most defensible for D1, D4 and D5; Reviewer C is most defensible for D2.

**D1 (randomization process).** Reviewer C's Low cannot stand. The article says patients were allocated "based on their birth dates… odd-numbered day… even-numbered day" (p.2).
- Box 4, 1.1 names this as a "No": "methods based on dates (of birth or admission)".
- §4.3.1 says that with systematic methods "concealing the allocation schedule is usually impossible". So 1.2 is N.
- Table 4 / Figure 1: 1.2 N/PN → High, whatever the answer to 1.3.

The best case for Low is the well-balanced baseline: 56 vs 54 patients, and similar pre-operative pivot-shift, KT-1000, Lysholm and IKDC values. But Box 4 says balance at baseline "should not influence answers to questions 1.1 or 1.2". Table 3 makes a judgement of Low conditional on "the allocation sequence was adequately concealed". I also considered overriding the default to Some concerns because the baseline is balanced. I rejected this. Anyone enrolling a patient knows their birth date, and the hypothesis favoured ALL reconstruction, so there was both the means and a reason to steer enrolment. §4.4 allows overrides when beliefs about benefit are weak, but that does not apply here. Reviewers A and B agree; I pick A.

**D2 (deviations from intended interventions, effect of assignment).** Reviewers A and B's Some concerns would need either 2.3 = NI (Part 1) or an inappropriate analysis (Part 2).
- **Part 2:** the analysis is by allocated group (53 of 56, 50 of 54). The only exclusions are patients who "left the country", i.e. missing outcome data. Box 6, 2.6 calls this kind of mITT analysis "appropriate", so Part 2 is Low.
- **Part 1:** Box 6, 2.3 notes that NI "may be appropriate, because trialists do not always report" deviations. Here, though, the flowchart reports "Intervention (n = 110)" and no crossovers. The surgery was a single procedure done once by one surgeon, and both groups had the same rehabilitation protocol. 2.3 requires "evidence, or strong reason to believe" before answering Y/PY. The evidence available points to protocol delivery, so PN is better supported than NI.

The unblinding of participants and the surgeon only makes 2.3 necessary; it does not lower the rating by itself (Table 6, row "Either 2.1 or 2.2 Y/PY/NI; 2.3 N/PN → Low"). The non-concealed allocation belongs to D1. The task told me not to carry it over, and Box 6 uses it only to answer 2.2, which is already Y. So I choose C (Low).

**D4 (measurement of the outcome).** The result being assessed includes Lysholm and IKDC as well as KT-1000. Lysholm is participant-reported (IKDC as well, if ref 7's subjective form is meant), and participants were unblinded ("we were not able to blind the participants", p.8).
- §7.1 (participant-reported outcomes): the assessment "is potentially influenced by knowledge of intervention received, leading to a judgement of at least 'Some concerns'".
- Box 10, 4.3: "For participant-reported outcomes, the outcome assessor is the study participant."

Reviewers B and C's Low is defensible only if the result were narrowed to the KT-1000 median alone. Even then, the white-stocking blinding of the examiner could be broken by unblinded patients (§7.3: the assessor is "considered to be aware… unless convincing evidence is available to the contrary"). The pivot-shift grading also involves examiner judgement. I also tested whether this should be High. It should not: both groups had active surgery, which §7.3 says carries lower risk than a no-treatment comparator. The patient-reported scores also showed no difference, so there is no reason to say influence was *likely* (Box 10, 4.5). So I choose A (Some concerns).

**D5 (selection of the reported result).** Reviewer C's Low is ruled out by the algorithm. Table 14 and Figure 7 reach Low only through 5.1 = Y/PY, i.e. data analysed according to a pre-specified plan finalised before unblinded data were available. No protocol, registry record or analysis plan exists in the files, so 5.1 is NI.

High would need clear evidence of selection based on the results (Box 11, 5.2/5.3). There are hints:
- Translation "at maximum pulling strength" is mentioned in the text but its full data are not reported.
- Only the final follow-up time point is reported.

These suggest other measurements existed but do not show selection. Against selection, every measure named in the Methods is reported, including the null results. Table 14 then gives Some concerns, from either row ("N/PN/NI, N/PN, N/PN" or "Any, NI, NI"). Reviewers A and B agree; I pick A.

CHOICE: D1=A; D2=C; D4=A; D5=A
REVISED: D1=High; D2=Low; D4=Some concerns; D5=Some concerns

My judgements are unchanged after trying to overturn each one: D1 High, D2 Low, D4 Some concerns, D5 Some concerns. Reviewer A is most defensible for D1, D4 and D5; Reviewer C is most defensible for D2.

**D1 (randomization process).** Reviewer C's Low cannot stand. The article says patients were allocated "based on their birth dates… odd-numbered day… even-numbered day" (p.2).
- Box 4, 1.1 names this as a "No": "methods based on dates (of birth or admission)".
- §4.3.1 says that with systematic methods "concealing the allocation schedule is usually impossible". So 1.2 is N.
- Table 4 / Figure 1: 1.2 N/PN → High, whatever the answer to 1.3.

The best case for Low is the well-balanced baseline: 56 vs 54 patients, and similar pre-operative pivot-shift, KT-1000, Lysholm and IKDC values. But Box 4 says balance at baseline "should not influence answers to questions 1.1 or 1.2". Table 3 makes a judgement of Low conditional on "the allocation sequence was adequately concealed". I also considered overriding the default to Some concerns because the baseline is balanced. I rejected this. Anyone enrolling a patient knows their birth date, and the hypothesis favoured ALL reconstruction, so there was both the means and a reason to steer enrolment. §4.4 allows overrides when beliefs about benefit are weak, but that does not apply here. Reviewers A and B agree; I pick A.

**D2 (deviations from intended interventions, effect of assignment).** Reviewers A and B's Some concerns would need either 2.3 = NI (Part 1) or an inappropriate analysis (Part 2).
- **Part 2:** the analysis is by allocated group (53 of 56, 50 of 54). The only exclusions are patients who "left the country", i.e. missing outcome data. Box 6, 2.6 calls this kind of mITT analysis "appropriate", so Part 2 is Low.
- **Part 1:** Box 6, 2.3 notes that NI "may be appropriate, because trialists do not always report" deviations. Here, though, the flowchart reports "Intervention (n = 110)" and no crossovers. The surgery was a single procedure done once by one surgeon, and both groups had the same rehabilitation protocol. 2.3 requires "evidence, or strong reason to believe" before answering Y/PY. The evidence available points to protocol delivery, so PN is better supported than NI.

The unblinding of participants and the surgeon only makes 2.3 necessary; it does not lower the rating by itself (Table 6, row "Either 2.1 or 2.2 Y/PY/NI; 2.3 N/PN → Low"). The non-concealed allocation belongs to D1. The task told me not to carry it over, and Box 6 uses it only to answer 2.2, which is already Y. So I choose C (Low).

**D4 (measurement of the outcome).** The result being assessed includes Lysholm and IKDC as well as KT-1000. Lysholm is participant-reported (IKDC as well, if ref 7's subjective form is meant), and participants were unblinded ("we were not able to blind the participants", p.8).
- §7.1 (participant-reported outcomes): the assessment "is potentially influenced by knowledge of intervention received, leading to a judgement of at least 'Some concerns'".
- Box 10, 4.3: "For participant-reported outcomes, the outcome assessor is the study participant."

Reviewers B and C's Low is defensible only if the result were narrowed to the KT-1000 median alone. Even then, the white-stocking blinding of the examiner could be broken by unblinded patients (§7.3: the assessor is "considered to be aware… unless convincing evidence is available to the contrary"). The pivot-shift grading also involves examiner judgement. I also tested whether this should be High. It should not: both groups had active surgery, which §7.3 says carries lower risk than a no-treatment comparator. The patient-reported scores also showed no difference, so there is no reason to say influence was *likely* (Box 10, 4.5). So I choose A (Some concerns).

**D5 (selection of the reported result).** Reviewer C's Low is ruled out by the algorithm. Table 14 and Figure 7 reach Low only through 5.1 = Y/PY, i.e. data analysed according to a pre-specified plan finalised before unblinded data were available. No protocol, registry record or analysis plan exists in the files, so 5.1 is NI.

High would need clear evidence of selection based on the results (Box 11, 5.2/5.3). There are hints:
- Translation "at maximum pulling strength" is mentioned in the text but its full data are not reported.
- Only the final follow-up time point is reported.

These suggest other measurements existed but do not show selection. Against selection, every measure named in the Methods is reported, including the null results. Table 14 then gives Some concerns, from either row ("N/PN/NI, N/PN, N/PN" or "Any, NI, NI"). Reviewers A and B agree; I pick A.

**D1 — A (equally B), High.** To challenge High, the reported groups have similar sizes and baseline characteristics (article p. 2, Figure 1; p. 3, Table 1). **D2 — C, Low.** A/B’s Some concerns could follow from answering 2.3=NI: participants and surgeons knew treatment, and detailed monitoring of deviations is absent. I reconsidered whether my earlier PN inferred too much from silence. Nevertheless, the article provides affirmative evidence of assigned surgery delivery for all 110 participants and describes a common rehabilitation regimen, including clinically indicated modifications for meniscal repair (pp. 2–4). Together these support PN, although not definitive N, for trial-context deviations. Box 6, 2.3 requires evidence or strong reason to attribute deviations to trial context; awareness alone is insufficient. Figure 1 and the outcome tables also support analysis by assignment, excluding only missing follow-up. Section 5.3.1 explicitly accepts such exclusions within D2. Figure 2 therefore gives Low through 2.3=PN and 2.6=PY.

**D4 — A, Some concerns.** B/C’s Low is persuasive for KT-1000 and pivot shift: a separate surgeon assessed patients with stockings concealing the operated knees (p. 2). That challenges any blanket claim of unblinded measurement. However, the requested result also includes subjective function, including Lysholm, and participants explicitly knew their treatment (p. 8). Box 10, 4.3 and §7.1 make the participant the assessor for participant-reported outcomes; a blinded examiner cannot remove that concern. Conversely, High would require likely influence, not merely possible influence. The active surgical comparator, separate examiner and approximately 27-month assessment support 4.5=PN under §7.3. This challenges an allegation of demonstrated selective reporting, but cannot establish prospective analysis intentions. No supplied protocol or dated analysis plan verifies decisions before unblinded data became available. Section 8.3.1 requires that timing, while Box 11, 5.2–5.3 specifies NI when intentions are insufficient and multiple measurements or analyses are possible. Figure 7 routes those NI answers to Some concerns. Neither multiple outcomes nor the significant KT-1000 result alone establishes High; A and B are equally defensible.

**D1 (randomization process).** Reviewer C's Low cannot stand. The article says patients were allocated "based on their birth dates… odd-numbered day… even-numbered day" (p.2).
- Box 4, 1.1 names this as a "No": "methods based on dates (of birth or admission)".
- §4.3.1 says that with systematic methods "concealing the allocation schedule is usually impossible". So 1.2 is N.
- Table 4 / Figure 1: 1.2 N/PN → High, whatever the answer to 1.3.

The best case for Low is the well-balanced baseline: 56 vs 54 patients, and similar pre-operative pivot-shift, KT-1000, Lysholm and IKDC values. But Box 4 says balance at baseline "should not influence answers to questions 1.1 or 1.2". Table 3 makes a judgement of Low conditional on "the allocation sequence was adequately concealed". I also considered overriding the default to Some concerns because the baseline is balanced. I rejected this. Anyone enrolling a patient knows their birth date, and the hypothesis favoured ALL reconstruction, so there was both the means and a reason to steer enrolment. §4.4 allows overrides when beliefs about benefit are weak, but that does not apply here. Reviewers A and B agree; I pick A.

**D2 (deviations from intended interventions, effect of assignment).** Reviewers A and B's Some concerns would need either 2.3 = NI (Part 1) or an inappropriate analysis (Part 2).
- **Part 2:** the analysis is by allocated group (53 of 56, 50 of 54). The only exclusions are patients who "left the country", i.e. missing outcome data. Box 6, 2.6 calls this kind of mITT analysis "appropriate", so Part 2 is Low.
- **Part 1:** Box 6, 2.3 notes that NI "may be appropriate, because trialists do not always report" deviations. Here, though, the flowchart reports "Intervention (n = 110)" and no crossovers. The surgery was a single procedure done once by one surgeon, and both groups had the same rehabilitation protocol. 2.3 requires "evidence, or strong reason to believe" before answering Y/PY. The evidence available points to protocol delivery, so PN is better supported than NI.

The unblinding of participants and the surgeon only makes 2.3 necessary; it does not lower the rating by itself (Table 6, row "Either 2.1 or 2.2 Y/PY/NI; 2.3 N/PN → Low"). The non-concealed allocation belongs to D1. The task told me not to carry it over, and Box 6 uses it only to answer 2.2, which is already Y. So I choose C (Low).

**D4 (measurement of the outcome).** The result being assessed includes Lysholm and IKDC as well as KT-1000. Lysholm is participant-reported (IKDC as well, if ref 7's subjective form is meant), and participants were unblinded ("we were not able to blind the participants", p.8).
- §7.1 (participant-reported outcomes): the assessment "is potentially influenced by knowledge of intervention received, leading to a judgement of at least 'Some concerns'".

## D2: Bias due to deviations from intended interventions

**I now choose C (Some concerns), which reverses my earlier Low.**

Reviewers A and B, like my first assessment, rest on answering 2.6 as PY. That answer treats the one excluded randomised patient as an mITT exclusion for missing outcome data. When I tried to break that reasoning, it failed:

- **Why the patient was excluded.** The reason was "SpO2 not recorded during intubation procedure" (Fig. 2). That is the primary outcome, not mortality.
- **Mortality was almost certainly known.** This is a single-centre ICU trial in which "mortality at day 28 will be recorded" (registry), so the patient's 28-day vital status was very likely available.
- **The guidance says where this belongs.** §6.1 states that bias from "other exclusions of eligible participants for whom outcome data are available, is addressed in the domain 'Bias due to deviations from intended interventions'". Box 6 (2.6) says "Analyses excluding eligible trial participants post-randomization should also be considered inappropriate." The patient was eligible, and the exclusion happened after randomisation.
- **The trial's own ITT definition is loose.** It allows exclusions for patients who "did not meet the inclusion criteria or improved before intubation" (p. 1881).

So 2.6 should be **PN**. For 2.7, the answer is **PN**:

- With the patient counted as dead, reference survival is 15/25 (60%); counted as alive, 16/25 (64%). Either way it is compared with 17/25 (68%).
- The patient's "intense peripheral vasoconstriction" may be prognostic, but this is still one patient out of 50.

Table 6, Part 2, row "2.6 N/PN/NI; 2.7 N/PN" gives **Some concerns**. Part 1 stays Low: operators were unblinded (2.2 Y), but 2.3 is PN.

I considered overriding to Low on the "material bias" principle (§1.2.1) and rejected it. The materiality question is exactly what 2.7 already asks. The algorithm still sends a 2.7 of PN to Some concerns, and §1.2.4 asks for reasons when departing from the algorithm. A small impact is not a reason to abandon the rubric's default.

**I keep A (Low).**

- 5.3: a binary death outcome compared with the planned chi-square/Fisher test has essentially one analysis, and both the ITT and per-protocol results are reported.

- §8.3.1 requires a "date-stamp" showing the plan was finalised before unblinded data were available.
- Only the 2017 version of the registry record is available, so its earliest wording cannot be confirmed.
- Mortality appears only in the registry's free-text description, not in the structured outcome fields.
- The protocol (ref 25) was published after the trial finished and is not provided.

Even so, the evidence supports a judgement of "Probably yes". §1.1 says the "Probably" responses "imply that a judgement has been made":

- The registry was first submitted on 2015-08-07, within weeks of the first enrolment and before almost any 28-day deaths could have been observed.

- What was reported matches it exactly.
- The abstract's "ICU mortality" label is a wording inconsistency, not a second result for the same outcome (§8.3.2(2)).

# RoB 2 assessment: Levin 2011, dronabinol vs placebo, two weeks of TLFB-reported abstinence in weeks 7–8 (ITT effect)

I judged D2 (deviations from intended interventions) and D4 (measurement of the outcome) as Low risk. D5 (selection of the reported result) has Some concerns, because I could not find an analysis plan that was dated before the data were unblinded.

**Preliminary considerations**
- **Design:** individually randomized, parallel-group, single-site trial.
- **Comparison:** dronabinol 20 mg twice daily (experimental) vs matching placebo (comparator).
- **Result assessed:** 14/79 (17.7%) vs 12/77 (15.6%), P = .69 (article p.144–145 §3.2; Table 2, p.146).
- **Sources:** the journal article and the ClinicalTrials.gov record NCT00217971 (including posted results). No protocol or statistical analysis plan was available.

## D2: Deviations from intended interventions (effect of assignment)

**Evidence for a concern:**
- Dronabinol is THC, and every participant was a daily cannabis user. They might recognise the drug's effects.
- More people on dronabinol reported feeling "uncomfortably intoxicated" (3 vs 1), and withdrawal scores fell more on dronabinol (p.147).
- The trial did not report any test of whether blinding held.

**Evidence against:**
- Capsules were matched: "All capsules looked identical for both treatment conditions" (p.143).
- Randomization was done by "A research pharmacist, who was independent of the research team" (p.143).
- Rates of any adverse effect were similar (67% vs 58%), and dose reductions were rare and spread across both arms (p.147).
- Most participants kept using cannabis, which would mask any effect of the study drug.

On balance I answered "Probably no" to awareness (2.1 and 2.2). The judgement would be the same with "Probably yes": nothing suggests deviations caused by the trial context. Adherence was similar (riboflavin fluorescence 100% vs 94%, P = .26), and dose changes followed the protocol rules. That would give 2.3 = "Probably no", which also leads to Low.

The analysis included everyone randomized (79 and 77 analysed), with missing data counted as cannabis use.

## D4: Measurement of the outcome

The outcome is self-reported through the timeline followback (TLFB), so the participant is the outcome assessor.
- The method is a pre-specified, standard measure. Self-report agreed with urine tests in the placebo arm (P = .003). Urine screens could not serve as the outcome because dronabinol itself turns them positive.
- The outcome was measured the same way in both arms: TLFB at twice-weekly visits.
- Participants were blinded by the matching placebo.

If someone judged that blinding failed, the route would be 4.3 = "Probably yes", 4.4 = "Probably yes", 4.5 = "Probably no", which gives Some concerns. I found no evidence that blinding failed in a way that would shape abstinence reports, so I kept Low.

## D5: Selection of the reported result

- The registered primary outcome matches the reported one: "Proportion of Patients Abstinent From Marijuana During Weeks 7 and 8", measured by TLFB.
- The paper also reports the alternative analyses, and every one of them is null:
  - the model-adjusted result;
  - a sensitivity analysis on missing data;
  - abstinence in each participant's last two weeks of participation (21.3% vs 19%);
  - maximum consecutive days of abstinence.
- However, the registry text about this outcome is in the past tense ("data was collected"). It reads as if it was written when results were posted in 2011, and no version history was provided.
- The rule that missing data count as cannabis use, and the mixed-model specification, appear only in the article.
- So I could not confirm a plan that was finalised before unblinding. Under the guidance that is "No information" for 5.1, which gives Some concerns. I did not override it.

# RoB 2 assessment: Levin 2011, dronabinol vs placebo, two weeks of TLFB-reported abstinence in weeks 7–8 (ITT effect)

I judged D2 (deviations from intended interventions) and D4 (measurement of the outcome) as Low risk. D5 (selection of the reported result) has Some concerns, because I could not find an analysis plan that was dated before the data were unblinded.

**Preliminary considerations**
- **Design:** individually randomized, parallel-group, single-site trial.
- **Comparison:** dronabinol 20 mg twice daily (experimental) vs matching placebo (comparator).
- **Result assessed:** 14/79 (17.7%) vs 12/77 (15.6%), P = .69 (article p.144–145 §3.2; Table 2, p.146).
- **Sources:** the journal article and the ClinicalTrials.gov record NCT00217971 (including posted results). No protocol or statistical analysis plan was available.

## D2: Deviations from intended interventions (effect of assignment)

**Evidence for a concern:**
- Dronabinol is THC, and every participant was a daily cannabis user. They might recognise the drug's effects.
- More people on dronabinol reported feeling "uncomfortably intoxicated" (3 vs 1), and withdrawal scores fell more on dronabinol (p.147).
- The trial did not report any test of whether blinding held.

**Evidence against:**
- Capsules were matched: "All capsules looked identical for both treatment conditions" (p.143).
- Randomization was done by "A research pharmacist, who was independent of the research team" (p.143).
- Rates of any adverse effect were similar (67% vs 58%), and dose reductions were rare and spread across both arms (p.147).
- Most participants kept using cannabis, which would mask any effect of the study drug.

On balance I answered "Probably no" to awareness (2.1 and 2.2). The judgement would be the same with "Probably yes": nothing suggests deviations caused by the trial context. Adherence was similar (riboflavin fluorescence 100% vs 94%, P = .26), and dose changes followed the protocol rules. That would give 2.3 = "Probably no", which also leads to Low.

The analysis included everyone randomized (79 and 77 analysed), with missing data counted as cannabis use.

## D4: Measurement of the outcome

The outcome is self-reported through the timeline followback (TLFB), so the participant is the outcome assessor.
- The method is a pre-specified, standard measure. Self-report agreed with urine tests in the placebo arm (P = .003). Urine screens could not serve as the outcome because dronabinol itself turns them positive.
- The outcome was measured the same way in both arms: TLFB at twice-weekly visits.
- Participants were blinded by the matching placebo.

If someone judged that blinding failed, the route would be 4.3 = "Probably yes", 4.4 = "Probably yes", 4.5 = "Probably no", which gives Some concerns. I found no evidence that blinding failed in a way that would shape abstinence reports, so I kept Low.

## D5: Selection of the reported result

- The registered primary outcome matches the reported one: "Proportion of Patients Abstinent From Marijuana During Weeks 7 and 8", measured by TLFB.
- The paper also reports the alternative analyses, and every one of them is null:
  - the model-adjusted result;
  - a sensitivity analysis on missing data;
  - abstinence in each participant's last two weeks of participation (21.3% vs 19%);
  - maximum consecutive days of abstinence.
- However, the registry text about this outcome is in the past tense ("data was collected"). It reads as if it was written when results were posted in 2011, and no version history was provided.
- The rule that missing data count as cannabis use, and the mixed-model specification, appear only in the article.
- So I could not confirm a plan that was finalised before unblinding. Under the guidance that is "No information" for 5.1, which gives Some concerns. I did not override it.
